newsitem.title: LEBANON: Army patrols Beirut as general strike starts.
newsitem.headline: Army patrols Beirut as general strike starts.

text.p: Schools and most shops closed in Beirut on Thursday in response to opposition calls for a general strike against Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri's policies but banks and financial markets opened for business as usual.

Troops in helmets and battle gear patrolled the capital and manned dozens of checkpoints, checking identity documents and sealing off parts of the city after the government outlawed a protest demonstration called by the opposition for 11 a.m. (0900 GMT).
Traffic during the normally frenzied weekday morning rush hour was reduced to a trickle.
Troops also patrolled other Lebanese cities, including Tripoli, Sidon and Tyre, the main cities of north and south Lebanon, where the strike appeared only partially effective.

A Reuter reporter in Sidon said about 40 percent of shops and schools and many banks closed. Schools also shut in Tripoli, but banks opened and most shopkeepers ignored the strike. In the southern city of Tyre schools were closed but banks opened and only 25 percent of shops were closed.

A broad spectrum of opposition groups backed by labour unions, students and media workers called the one-day strike in protest at Hariri's policy towards the media, his perceived lack of concern for social issues and a standing ban on public demonstrations.

The protest shut down much of Beirut hours after Hariri's new government won a confidence vote in parliament by a comfortable 102-19 margin after a bruising three-day debate in which a handful of prominent opposition deputies grabbed the limelight.
Hariri responded to the criticisms by telling the house that his government had improved the Lebanese economy dramatically in the past four years.

The central bank opened for business as usual and most commercial banks opened to the public after initial hesitation. The Beirut Stock Exchange also opened and banks' foreign exchange dealers were at their posts.

Beirut airport was open as normal. Employees of Middle East Airlines, the national carrier, planned a symbolic one-hour stoppage from 11 a.m. to noon (0900-1000 GMT) that was not expected to affect air traffic.
The protests were galvanised by a government decision to shut scores of private radio and television stations by Saturday, which the opposition calls an attack on Lebanese liberties.
All opposition radio and television stations will close under a new law regulating the audiovisual media.
Only a few stations belonging to or controlled by Hariri and other establishment figures have been granted licences in what the opposition calls a carve-up of the audiovisual market.
The government has banned the planned demonstration in Beirut and says the army and security forces will keep order.
Troops sealed off the prime minister's offices and the area where the demonstration was due to take place.
The pro-Iranian Hizbollah (Party of God), whose deputies voted against Hariri in Wednesday's confidence vote, has called on its supporters to back the strike and demonstration.
Its decision raised the possibility that thousands of Shi'ite Moslem militants could pour into the streets to join the demonstration.
In a last minute appeal, strike organisers accused Hariri, who has set Lebanon on the road to postwar recovery, of suppressing media freedoms and imposing a "dictatorship of impoverishment."

"Hariri's government has led one third of the Lebanese people to poverty and confiscated the free media and has banned demonstrations in order to impose his regime and protect his partners' control on Lebanon," they said.
